THOUGHT: The patient is a 42-year-old man with visible hematuria and right flank pain, plus a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Urinalysis shows gross hematuria (RBCs too numerous to count) with pyuria (WBC 10–20/HPF) and positive leukocyte esterase but negative nitrites, consistent with urinary tract infection/inflammation but not pointing to a specific nitrite-producing organism. Renal function is preserved (creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL). The key diagnostic clue is the intravenous pyelogram describing multiple cysts in the collecting ducts of the renal medulla with no obstruction—this radiographic appearance is characteristic of medullary sponge kidney (MSK), a congenital cystic dilatation of the collecting ducts that often presents in adulthood with hematuria, recurrent UTIs, nephrolithiasis, and normal-to-near-normal renal function. Other considerations (renal stone, malignancy, papillary necrosis, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) are less likely given the imaging description (medullary collecting-duct cysts without obstruction and preserved kidney function) and the clinical history. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is medullary sponge kidney, which explains the recurrent infections, hematuria, and imaging findings.

DIAGNOSIS: Medullary sponge kidney (congenital cystic dilatation of medullary collecting ducts)
